stimulus.text: Historian William Leuchtenburg argues the New Deal 'vastly enlarged the power of the presidency and the scope of federal responsibility' — a revolution in government's role that both major parties would spend the rest of the century debating.

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE way government expanded to combat the Great Depression.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of that expansion.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of resistance to the expansion of government in the 1930s.
exemplar: Hoover created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932) to lend to banks and businesses, breaking with pure voluntarism.
Roosevelt's Hundred Days vastly expanded Washington: the AAA, CCC, TVA, and FDIC put the federal government into farming, employment, power, and banking.
Resistance came from both sides: business leaders denounced the New Deal as socialism (the Liberty League), while the Supreme Court struck down the NRA and AAA in 1935–36.
Adams urges her husband and the Continental Congress to grant women legal rights and protections in the new republic, warning that women will rebel against laws in which they have no voice.
The Revolution's rhetoric of natural rights and consent of the governed gave women like Adams a language to demand that republican principles apply to them as well as to men.

Within a few years, states such as New Jersey briefly allowed propertied women to vote, and the Revolution spurred expanded educational opportunities for girls - though coverture law kept married women legally subordinate.
parts: A. Briefly describe what Adams asks of her husband and the Continental Congress in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE reason the American Revolution encouraged some women to demand greater rights.
C. Briefly explain ONE way women's status did change as a result of the Revolution.

stimulus.text: Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could.

exemplar: The photograph captures the peaceful, massive scale of the demonstration - ordinary people filling the capital's public space - which signaled that the movement spoke for the nation, not a fringe.
The march pressured the federal government: within a year Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, outlawing segregation in public places and employment discrimination.

Critics argued the march's orderliness muted its radicalism - Malcolm X dismissed it as the 'Farce on Washington' - and that legislation alone did not end de facto segregation in housing, schools, or jobs.

C. Briefly explain ONE criticism of the march or of its achievements.

stimulus.attribution: Described from the 1963 photograph of the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom (National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons).
stimulus.text: The photograph shows an enormous, densely packed crowd stretching from the Lincoln Memorial toward the Washington Monument - men, women, and children of many races, many holding signs demanding jobs and freedom. The demonstration is orderly and peaceful despite its vast size.
